clue.text: Through family feud, sign provided for would-be king

blocks.note: per means through or by way of, as in 'per post'
kin are one's relatives
a feud is a war between families
a beck is a beckoning gesture, as in 'at someone's beck and call'

explanation.surface: A pretender to the throne gets his chance through a quarrel within a royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: Perkin Warbeck claimed to be one of the Princes in the Tower and tried to seize the English crown from Henry VII in the 1490s.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a famous pretender to the English throne, a claimant who never actually reigned.

clue.text: Having served with patrol, one repeatedly given order

definitions.text: Having served with patrol, one repeatedly given order

indicators.note: letters given a fresh order are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged
one is I, and repeated gives it twice

explanation.surface: A veteran of patrols, someone constantly ordered about.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a soldier of the lowest rank who goes out on patrol and is forever being given orders.
explanation.definitionFit: A private is the lowest rank in the army, serving on patrols and constantly receiving commands from superiors.

clue.text: Warning system run by playschool?

blocks.note: RADA is the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London, a school for plays
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A warning system operated by a nursery school, as if toddlers kept watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playschool' suggests a nursery for toddlers; read as play school, it is a drama academy. The question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Radar detects approaching aircraft or ships by radio echoes, giving early warning of them.

clue.text: Nice bride left in distress — extraordinary!

indicators.note: in distress suggests being thrown into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A pleasant bride is jilted and upset, an astonishing turn of events.
explanation.definitionFit: Incredible means hard to believe, so remarkable or astonishing that it seems beyond the ordinary.

clue.text: Brought up fresh rations for combat

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: raw means fresh, uncooked or new
fare is food provided, rations

explanation.surface: New supplies are delivered to troops for battle.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the turnaround applies only to the first piece; the rations follow in normal order.
explanation.definitionFit: Warfare is the activity of fighting a war, armed combat between forces.

clue.text: Type of, say, foreign royal once

blocks.note: roman is the ordinary upright style of printing type
the Russian surname ending -ov means 'of', as in son of

explanation.surface: Asking about the kind of foreign royal there used to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' is the printer's sense: roman as opposed to italic. The foreign 'of' fits the Russian dynasty in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romanovs were the ruling dynasty of Russia until the Revolution of 1917, so its members were royals in the past.

clue.text: Executed poem in this language

indicators.note: an executed person may be beheaded, so the word loses its head, its first letter

blocks.note: a verse is a poem or piece of poetry

explanation.surface: A poem was carried out in a particular language.
explanation.walkthrough: VERSE without its V. 'This language' points at the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic tongue of Scotland or Ireland.

clue.text: Decisive blows — only the very best survive them

definitions.text: only the very best survive them

blocks.note: first meaning: punches that end a boxing bout

blocks.clueFragment: only the very best survive them
blocks.note: second meaning: elimination competitions where losers drop out each round

explanation.walkthrough: The second half sounds like it continues the boxing picture, but it describes a tournament format such as a cup competition.
explanation.definitionFit: A knockout is a punch that floors an opponent, and also a tournament in which each loser is eliminated.

clue.text: Obstacle created by second collapsing building

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
tumbling means falling down
a block is a large building, as in a block of flats

explanation.surface: A building falling down for a moment creates an obstruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collapsing' looks like an anagram signal but simply means falling.
explanation.definitionFit: A stumbling-block is something that gets in the way of progress, an impediment or hindrance.

clue.text: A lot of codeine mixed with alcohol produces improper behaviour

indicators.note: a lot of something is not quite all of it, so the word loses its final letter
mixed suggests the letters are stirred up into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, then cut short
rum is a kind of alcoholic spirit

explanation.surface: Taking too many painkillers with drink leads to bad behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last E of CODEINE, rearrange the rest to INDECO, then add RUM.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecorum is a lack of propriety, conduct that breaks the rules of polite manners.

clue.text: Having beer belly from drink

blocks.note: first meaning: fat, portly
second meaning: a dark, strong beer

explanation.surface: Someone has grown a paunch from drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the drink the cause of the belly; the word is both the portly build and a dark beer such as Guinness.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a portly, heavily built person and is also the name of a dark heavy beer.

clue.text: Concede match

blocks.note: first meaning: to admit a point is right
second meaning: to correspond or tally

explanation.surface: A sportsman gives up a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concede match' reads as giving up a game, but the two words are separate meanings of one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To agree is both to grant that someone is right and for two things to be consistent with each other.

clue.text: Bristly parts cut from front of grassy areas

indicators.note: cutting from the front means the opening letter is removed

blocks.note: lawns are areas of mown grass

explanation.surface: Spiky bits are trimmed off the edge of some lawns.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the L at the front of LAWNS.
explanation.definitionFit: Awns are the stiff bristles growing from the ears of grasses such as barley.

clue.text: Read superficially the beginning of Scarlett O'Hara

indicators.note: the beginning of a name is just its opening letter

blocks.note: first letter of the name
Kim O'Hara is the boy hero of Kipling's novel Kim

explanation.surface: Someone only glances at the opening of Gone with the Wind's heroine's story.
explanation.walkthrough: Scarlett O'Hara pulls the eye to Gone with the Wind, but O'Hara stands alone for another O'Hara: Kipling's Kim.
explanation.definitionFit: To skim a text is to glance through it quickly without taking in the detail.

clue.text: They do some paperwork — when not busy with punctures?

definitions.note: a cryptic description read as free lances

blocks.note: first meaning: self-employed journalists writing for newspapers
second meaning: spears that are free, not engaged in piercing anything

explanation.walkthrough: 'Paperwork' means writing for papers, not office forms; the question mark flags the punning second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Freelances are self-employed writers selling articles to several newspapers rather than working on staff.

clue.text: Interweave ten pieces, finishing up with sack, perhaps

indicators.note: broken into pieces, the word's letters can be put back in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
sack is an old name for a dry fortified wine like sherry; 'perhaps' marks it as one example

explanation.surface: Instructions for weaving ten strands, ending with a bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sack' looks like a bag, but here it is the old fortified wine Falstaff loved.
explanation.definitionFit: To entwine is to twist things together, which is what interweaving strands does.

clue.text: Long-haired fellow endlessly pushed around in the Treasury

indicators.note: endlessly means the word loses its last letter
around means one piece goes about the other, enclosing it

blocks.note: Esau in Genesis was a hairy man, unlike his brother Jacob
thrust means pushed forcefully

explanation.surface: A hippie was shoved around inside the government finance department.
explanation.walkthrough: Esau is the conventional hairy man of the Bible. 'Treasury' looks like Britain's finance ministry, but it is the old sense of a store of treasures.
explanation.definitionFit: Thesaurus comes from the Greek word for a treasure-house, and a word-book is a store of vocabulary.

clue.text: Practical morality not quite achieved by a learner

indicators.note: not quite all there means the word stops one letter short

blocks.note: virtue is moral goodness
taken as written
L is the learner-driver plate

explanation.surface: A beginner nearly manages to be good in a practical way.
explanation.walkthrough: VIRTUE loses its last E before A and L are added.
explanation.definitionFit: Virtual means being so in effect or in practice, though not formally or strictly.

clue.text: Extend beyond closed circuit

blocks.note: something over is finished or closed
a lap is one circuit of a track

explanation.surface: A racing circuit is extended beyond its closed loop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Closed circuit' reads as a single phrase, as in CCTV, but it splits into two words that each give a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: When one thing overlaps another it reaches past its edge and covers part of it.

clue.text: Rod and whip needed for wild animal

blocks.note: a pole is a long rod
the cat is the cat-o'-nine-tails, a flogging whip

explanation.surface: A rod and a whip are what a lion tamer needs for a wild beast.
explanation.definitionFit: A polecat is a dark-furred wild carnivore of the weasel family, known for its smell.

clue.text: Turncoat's initial cause for disloyalty

indicators.note: the initial of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of the word
a reason is a cause or motive

explanation.surface: Asking what first drove a defector to betray his side.
explanation.definitionFit: Treason is the crime of betraying one's own country, the gravest disloyalty.

clue.text: The sort of deal that gets lower classes into coach

indicators.note: getting something into another puts it inside

blocks.note: to coach someone is to train them
D and E are the lowest grades in the British social classification used by market researchers

explanation.surface: A cheap deal that puts working-class passengers into a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like a vehicle but is the verb train, which takes DE inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade-in deal is one where an old item is handed over as part payment for a new one.

clue.text: Face setback

indicators.note: going back means reading the word from its end to its start

blocks.note: the first part, set, means laid, as a table is laid; the attached back is the turnaround signal

explanation.surface: Someone confronts a reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setback' reads as one word for a reverse, but it splits: set is the wordplay, back the turnaround signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dial is the face of a clock or watch, the part bearing the numbers.

clue.text: Circus performer for the high jump

definitions.text: Circus performer for the high jump

blocks.clueFragment: Circus performer for the high jump
blocks.note: surface reading: a circus act about to be punished, 'for the high jump' meaning in serious trouble

blocks.clueFragment: Circus performer for the high jump
blocks.note: setter's reading: a tiny trained insect in a sideshow circus, celebrated for leaping many times its own height

explanation.walkthrough: 'For the high jump' is British slang for being in trouble; read literally it describes the insect's leap.
explanation.definitionFit: Flea circuses were sideshows where trained insects appeared to perform, and these insects are prodigious jumpers.

clue.text: A daughter, born after '51, unplanned

indicators.note: after tells us the piece for born is placed second, behind the number

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
LI is 51 in Roman numerals
B is the abbreviation for born

explanation.surface: A daughter arrived in the fifties without being planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Born after' puts B behind LI.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad lib describes something improvised, spoken or done without preparation.

clue.text: Breather one takes in a loincloth

blocks.note: a lung is the organ we breathe with
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone pausing for breath wears only a loincloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breather' looks like a rest but is the organ that breathes.
explanation.definitionFit: A lungi is a length of cloth wrapped around the waist, worn by men in South Asia.

clue.text: Nearly discharge troops for protest

indicators.note: nearly the whole word means it stops one letter short

blocks.note: demob is short for demobilise, to release soldiers from service

explanation.surface: Almost releasing soldiers from service as a protest.
explanation.definitionFit: A demo is a public demonstration, a march or rally voicing objection to something.

clue.text: Weird source of effluent in lake

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it begins, its first letter
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: first letter of the word
Lake Erie is one of North America's Great Lakes

explanation.surface: A strange outflow is discovered polluting a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The E goes inside ERIE after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerie means strange and unsettling, uncanny in a way that makes one uneasy.

clue.text: After dreadful scene by councillor party is getting noisier

indicators.note: something dreadful is in a bad state, so the word's letters are jumbled

blocks.note: Cr is the abbreviation for councillor
taken as written, to be rearranged
a do is a party

explanation.surface: After a councillor makes an ugly scene, a party grows louder.
explanation.walkthrough: Cr is a common abbreviation for councillor in British local government; 'After' and 'by' only fix the order of the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In music a crescendo marks a passage gradually growing louder, an adverbial sense matching the phrase.

clue.text: Single-seater hitting flak

blocks.note: shooting at a target is aiming to hit it
in British slang, to give someone stick is to criticise them, as flak is criticism

explanation.surface: A single-seat fighter plane is struck by anti-aircraft fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single-seater' and 'flak' summon a fighter plane; the seat is the fold-out one on a walking stick used at race meetings.
explanation.definitionFit: A shooting stick is a spiked walking stick whose handle unfolds into a seat for one person.
